headline: The U.S. loses its measles-free status after 26 years

sources.title: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers (BBC News)
US loses measles elimination status amid worst outbreak since 1991 (The Guardian)
PAHO urges countries to step up efforts to stop measles outbreaks and move towards elimination in the Americas (Pan American Health Organization)
Measles in the Americas: Questions and Answers, Technical Reference for Journalists and the Public (Pan American Health Organization)

chunks.text: The U.S. has lost a [[public health]] title that it held for 26 years. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization, the World Health Organization's office for the Americas, said the U.S., Mexico and Bolivia no longer have measles [[elimination status]]. That status means the disease does not spread [[nonstop]] in a country. Measles is a highly [[contagious]] disease. One sick person can {{pass it on}} to as many as 18 [[unprotected]] people. The organization [[urged]] countries to {{step up}} efforts to stop it.

verbs.correct: To give a disease to someone else
verbs.wrong: To test someone for a disease
verbs.why: Parents often pass colds on to their children. A sick cook can pass on a stomach virus to many customers. One person with measles can pass it on to as many as 18 people who are not protected.
Schools step up safety checks before big events. Police step up patrols during large festivals. The organization urged countries to step up their efforts to stop measles.

chunks.text: Travelers can still bring the virus home, and [[outbreaks]], groups of cases in one place, can {{flare up}}. A country keeps its status if each outbreak {{dies out}} within 12 months. It loses the status when the same [[strain]], or type, of the virus spreads nonstop for a full year. The U.S. outbreak began on January 20, 2025, and {{dragged on}} past the [[one-year mark]], the organization said.

verbs.why: Small fires flare up in dry summer weather. Flu cases often flare up in crowded schools. Measles outbreaks can still flare up in a country that has elimination status.
Many small languages die out when children stop learning them. An old custom dies out when nobody practices it. A country keeps its status if each outbreak dies out within 12 months.
Some meetings drag on all afternoon. A bad cold often drags on for weeks. The American outbreak began in January 2025 and dragged on past the one-year mark.

chunks.text: Cases have {{shot up}} across the Americas. The organization counted 58,213 by November 13, 2026, compared with 12,806 at the same point in 2025. It [[blamed]] [[gaps]] in vaccination. The CDC, the U.S. health agency, counted 5,412 American cases by that date. State [[health departments]] reported 10 deaths linked to measles in 2026. The country's measles [[vaccination rate]] has {{gone down}} to 92.4 percent. Some Americans are being asked to {{dig up}} old [[vaccination records]].

verbs.why: Ticket prices shoot up before a big game. Gas prices often shoot up in the summer. Measles cases have shot up across the Americas.

verbs.wrong: To be sold at a clinic
verbs.why: Prices often go down after the summer. The number of visitors goes down in winter. The American measles vaccination rate has gone down to 92.4 percent.

verbs.correct: To find something old by searching
verbs.wrong: To sell something to a doctor
verbs.why: She digs up old family photos for the party. He digs up his school records for a new job. Some Americans are being asked to dig up old vaccination records.

chunks.text: The three countries must now {{turn in}} plans that {{spell out}} how they will raise vaccination rates. To {{win back}} the title, each must show that the spread has stopped for at least 12 months [[in a row]]. The CDC said it is [[committed]] to that goal. The organization's director said elimination is not a [[trophy]] that a country wins once. Countries must work every day to {{hold on to}} it.

verbs.correct: To give finished work to someone
verbs.wrong: To read something to a sick child
verbs.why: Students turn in their homework on Friday. Workers turn in their reports every month. The three countries must now turn in plans to the organization.

verbs.wrong: To send a bill to a doctor
verbs.why: The coach spells out the plan before each game. A good teacher spells out the rules on the first day. The plans must spell out how each country will raise its vaccination rate.

verbs.correct: To get something again after losing it
verbs.wrong: To print something on a health card
verbs.why: The store tries to win back old customers with low prices. The team wants to win back the title next season. To win back the title, a country must show that the spread has stopped for at least 12 months in a row.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose it
verbs.wrong: To buy something a second time
verbs.why: Good companies try to hold on to their best workers. Families work hard to hold on to their homes. The director said countries must work every day to hold on to elimination status.

wordDefs.def: The work of keeping all the people in a place healthy
ex: She studied public health in college.

ex: Experts review a country's elimination status every year.

wordDefs.def: Able to spread from one person to another
ex: Stay home if you are still contagious.

wordDefs.def: Not kept safe from harm or disease
ex: Unprotected skin burns quickly in the sun.

wordDefs.def: Strongly asked someone to do something

wordDefs.def: Times when a disease suddenly affects many people

wordDefs.def: One type of a virus or germ
ex: This flu strain makes people very tired.

The vaccine protects against more than one strain.

wordDefs.def: The point when exactly one year has passed

wordDefs.def: Said that someone or something caused a problem

wordDefs.def: One after another, with no break

wordDefs.def: A prize, often a metal cup, given to a winner

mainIdea.s: The U.S., Mexico and Bolivia lost a health title because one measles strain kept spreading for over a year. Each country must now raise vaccination and prove that the virus has stopped.
mainIdea.why: The same strain spread nonstop for at least 12 months. The countries must turn in plans and show that the spread has stopped.

mainIdea.s: One sick traveler from abroad is enough to cost a nation this health title under the rules. That is why three countries in the Americas lost it after a few visitors arrived with measles.
mainIdea.why: Close, but outbreaks from travelers can flare up without any loss of status. A country loses it when one strain spreads nonstop for a full year.

mainIdea.s: A new measles vaccine has passed its final tests and should reach clinics across the Americas next spring. Doctors expect this single shot to replace the two doses that children receive today.
mainIdea.why: No new vaccine is described here. Three countries lost their status, and they must now turn in plans to stop the spread.

tf.s: Measles cases have shot up across the Americas.
tf.why: Cases have shot up to 58,213, far more than at the same point in 2025.

tf.s: Mexico and Bolivia held on to their measles elimination status.
tf.why: Neither country could hold on to the status. Both lost it along with the U.S.

tf.s: Measles outbreaks can flare up in a country with elimination status.
tf.why: Travelers can still bring the virus home and start an outbreak.

tf.s: The three countries must turn in plans to raise vaccination rates.
tf.why: They must turn in plans that explain how they will raise those rates.

tf.s: A country loses its status when an outbreak dies out quickly.
tf.why: A country keeps its status if each outbreak dies out within 12 months. It loses the status when one strain spreads for a full year.

tf.s: Once a country loses the title, it can never win it back.
tf.why: A country can win back the title by showing that the spread has stopped for at least 12 months in a row.

lines.text: Did you see that the U.S. lost its measles elimination status?
I did. It sounds like [[a step backward]]. Does it mean everyone is catching measles now?
No. Outbreaks can {{flare up}} in any country. The problem is that one {{dragged on}} for more than a year.
Right. The same strain kept spreading, and that cost the country its title.
No, Mexico and Bolivia lost it too. Cases have {{shot up}} all over the Americas.
[[That can't be good]]. Measles is so easy to {{pass on}}.
I know. [[On top of that]], the U.S. vaccination rate has {{gone down}}.
Is that why people are talking about their old shots?
Yes. Some people are being asked to {{dig up}} old vaccination records.
I don't know where mine are.
[[Same here]]. I should call my doctor.
Can the country {{win back}} the title?
Yes, but first it has to {{turn in}} a plan and stop the spread for 12 months.
No. And after that, it has to work to {{hold on to}} it.

expressions.def: A change that makes things worse than before
ex: Closing the library would be a step backward for our town.

expressions.def: Used when you think something will cause a problem
ex: The car is making a strange noise. That can't be good.

expressions.def: Used to add one more fact, often a bad one
ex: I lost my keys. On top of that, it started to rain.

expressions.def: Used to say that the same is true for you
ex: "I'm so tired today." "Same here."

expressions.def: Used to say that something will take a long time
ex: Learning a language won't happen overnight.
Change won't happen overnight, but we can start today.
